newsitem.title: USA: Levitt disturbed by "eminent domain" bond calls.
newsitem.headline: Levitt disturbed by "eminent domain" bond calls.

text.p: SEC Chairman Arthur Levitt said Friday he is disturbed that some localities are using "eminent domain" as an excuse to call bonds in an effort to refinance oustanding debt.

"A handful of small issuers have tried using this strategy recently, as an end-run around restrictions that otherwise prevent them from calling their bonds," Levitt said in a speech before bond issuers in Albany, N.Y. "These townships don't demolish public buildings -- but they do demolish the public trust."

Levitt was referring to a controversial move by a New Jersey school district last fall to use the power of eminent domain to condemn school buildings that secure over $3 million in lease-backed securities as part of a plan to call the bonds at par.

Also, bondholders in a small Colorado town have sued city officials for condemning city hall in order to refund certificates of participation at par. Investors said the call feature was inadequately disclosed in the official statement.
Levitt said that by using the strategy, localities "erode trust" and "callously break faith with their bondholders."

"Such short-sighted maneuvers jeopardize the municipal market's hard-earned reputation for credit quality," Levitt said in his luncheon speech before the New York State Government Finance Officers Association.

"That reputation assures issuers of a receptive market for their offerings and thus an efficient source of funds," he said. "If commerce runs on certainty and contract, it follows that the most harmful thing that could happen to our markets is to breach that trust.

"The resulting skepticism erodes trust for all. Eminent domain deals may save issuers a few basis points -- but they come at the cost of the investors who bought the original bonds, not to mention the market itself."
